findings.explanation: Construction (lines 81-92) rejects a negative capacity with Assert.isTrue, hence IllegalArgumentException, and otherwise stores the capacity and generator and creates a ConcurrentHashMap with initial capacity 16, load factor 0.75, and concurrency-level hint 16. That hint is not a generation or update concurrency ceiling. At capacity zero, get directly returns generator.apply(key): it never consults or changes the map or buffers, so even a null generator result is returned, and a thrown exception propagates unchanged. At positive capacity, a hit records a read on the fetched node and returns that node's value. A miss invokes the generator before put and outside evictionLock. There is no per-key single-flight behavior, so competing misses can generate concurrently. Their putIfAbsent calls choose one published node: its caller queues AddTask, while every loser records a read on the winning prior node. Nevertheless, get returns its own local generated value, so a loser can return a value different from the value retained in the cache. With the assumed non-null key, a positive-capacity null result reaches Assert.notNull(value) and throws IllegalArgumentException before insertion. Generator failures are not caught and likewise perform no insertion. Generation therefore has no cache-imposed serialization; only publication of the winning node is atomic.

processRead is used both for ordinary hits and for a putIfAbsent loser, with the latter recording the winning prior node. recordRead (lines 367-415) selects one of four buffers using the low two bits of the current thread ID. Each is a bounded 128-slot ring. It advances that buffer's recorded count, stores the node lazily, and computes the prior backlog as recordedCount minus processedCount. A backlog below 32 is reported as delayable; at 32 or more an IDLE reader attempts maintenance. Recording does not itself reorder the eviction queue. The outer drain visits all four buffers, beginning at a buffer selected by the draining thread. The quoted helper snapshots recordedCount, consumes at most 64 slots per buffer, stops at the first null slot, clears each consumed slot, increments readCount, and finally publishes processedCount as the initial snapshot even if the loop stopped early or reached its bound. moveToBack changes the queue only when the node is currently linked and is not already the tail; unlinked nodes are ignored and the existing tail is unchanged. Actual queue mutation is serialized by evictionLock, but reads are first placed into independent, bounded, lazily published rings and drains traverse buffers rather than a single global chronology. A drain may also be delayed or lose tryLock. Consequently, read recording provides deferred approximate recency, not one synchronous, globally ordered LRU mutation for every access.

Every write task is first appended to a ConcurrentLinkedQueue, then status is set to REQUIRED and that caller attempts a drain. For reads, the boolean returned by recordRead is semantically “delayable” despite the local name: IDLE drains only when it is false, REQUIRED always attempts a drain, and PROCESSING suppresses another attempt. drainOperations uses nonblocking tryLock. Failure simply returns; buffered work remains for the current lock holder if observed in time or for a later calling thread. There is no worker or executor performing maintenance in the background. A successful drainer sets PROCESSING, drains all read buffers first, then runs at most 16 queued write tasks during a normal drain. This bound can leave tasks pending until another read/write trigger. In finally, compareAndSet changes PROCESSING to IDLE and the lock is always released. If a concurrent writer changed PROCESSING to REQUIRED, the CAS fails and preserves REQUIRED so a later caller will retry. The lock serializes queue reordering, write-task execution, accounting, and eviction; it does not surround generation, map get/putIfAbsent/remove, read recording, or every public observation.

The winning putIfAbsent changes the public backing map before it queues AddTask, so size/contains can observe the node before queue membership or currentSize accounting. The task is buffered, although its caller may execute it immediately if tryLock succeeds. AddTask increments currentSize even if the node has meanwhile ceased to be ACTIVE; an inactive node is not queued or used to trigger eviction, and its queued removal work performs the corresponding cleanup. An active node is appended at the queue back and eviction runs while internal currentSize exceeds capacity. It repeatedly polls the oldest queued node, exits if the queue is empty even when accounting is still over capacity, and uses cache.remove(key, node), so a newer same-key mapping is not removed by evicting an old node. markAsRemoved (lines 203-211) repeatedly snapshots the entry, constructs a REMOVED entry retaining exactly the same value, and after a successful CAS decrements currentSize; it does not clear the value. currentSize is therefore maintenance accounting, distinct from ConcurrentHashMap.size(), which backs the public size(). Map insertion/removal can precede accounting, and writes or recency records can await a lock or a later bounded drain. Capacity enforcement and queue mutation are serialized under evictionLock when maintenance runs, but public map size and LRU order are not instantaneous strict guarantees.

remove first removes the current mapping directly from the concurrent map. An absent key returns false without state or queue work; a present mapping becomes immediately absent to size(), contains(), and new map lookups, and remove returns true. markForRemoval preserves the value while conditionally changing ACTIVE to PENDING_REMOVAL. It retries if the CAS loses and exits without another transition if the observed entry is already inactive. RemovalTask (lines 293-305) is then queued; under evictionLock it unlinks the node if still present in the eviction queue and invokes markAsRemoved for REMOVED state and currentSize cleanup. That maintenance is deferred when tryLock fails, though it can complete synchronously in the removing caller when the lock is available. Immediate map invisibility therefore precedes potentially deferred queue/state/accounting work. Removal does not cancel or invalidate a retrieval that obtained the old node before the map removal: all state transitions retain its value, and that retrieval may still record the node and return the old value.

Unlike ordinary maintenance, clear takes evictionLock with blocking lock() and releases it in finally. It polls every currently queued node, identity-conditionally removes that node from the map, and marks it REMOVED with accounting decrement. It next nulls every read-buffer slot; ReadOperations.clear (lines 426-433) does not reset recordedCount, readCount, or processedCount. Finally it uses drainAll, which has no 16-task bound and runs queued write tasks until a poll observes none. clear never calls cache.clear(). A mapping whose AddTask has not yet linked it is absent from the initial queue walk, and draining that queued addition can link it during clear rather than remove it. Concurrent map operations also do not acquire evictionLock: a concurrent insertion or same-key replacement can remain, identity-conditional removal protects a replacement, and work enqueued after drainAll observes an empty queue can remain pending. Thus the lock serializes maintenance against other drains, but clear is not an unconditional atomic-empty barrier against concurrent map changes or queued additions. size() returns the concurrent backing map's current mapping count; contains(key) asks that map directly; capacity() returns the immutable configured bound; deprecated sizeLimit() returns the same bound. The sequential tests in src/test/java/org/springframework/util/ConcurrentLruCacheTests.java corroborate zero-capacity bypass (lines 34-55), insertion/eviction (57-73), removal (75-91), and clear followed by reuse (93-109). They exercise one thread and therefore do not prove concurrent generation, ordering, capacity, or clearing guarantees.
